routes.description: Establish that contingent reality requires an explanation outside the totality of contingent things, that this explanatory foundation exists necessarily, and that its comparative explanatory virtues support identifying it as God.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if contingency remains distinct from causal determination, the explanatory principle applies to the plurality of contingent things without an illicit composition inference, and a perfect necessary being is supported over a necessary-universe terminus.

motionBridge.description: Connect the necessary foundation of contingent reality to God through a warranted deductive or abductive identification.

centralBridges.description: Establish that reality includes genuinely contingent things whose existence calls for explanation despite any deterministic causal history.
Show that explaining contingent things individually or through their plurality does not remove the need for a non-contingent explanatory foundation.
Show that simplicity, absence of arbitrary limits, or cumulative theistic considerations favor a perfect necessary being over a necessary universe.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Clarify the relationship between modal contingency, existential dependence, causal determination, and explanatory need.
Ground the demand for explanation in ordinary inquiry, scientific practice, induction, or the stable order of reality.

routes.description: Block the theistic contingency inference by challenging the establishment of genuine contingency, the move from contingent members to an external foundation, and the identification of any necessary reality as God rather than the universe.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if determinism or a necessary-universe option remains viable, if the totality-level explanatory demand is unsupported, or if the proposed divine terminus lacks a non-question-begging advantage over non-theistic necessary reality.

motionBridge.description: Show that the argument does not establish a distinct necessary foundation with attributes sufficient for identification as God.

centralBridges.description: Require justification that observed things could have existed differently and test whether determinism transmits necessity through the causal order.
Show that moving from explanations of contingent members to an explanation outside their totality may assume composition or explanatory convergence.
Preserve a necessary or brute universe as an alternative explanatory terminus and test whether it is at least as simple as a divine foundation.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Require a principled distinction between treating God as necessarily self-explanatory and allowing comparable treatment of non-divine reality.
Examine whether perfection, unlimited power, divine will, or theological complexity supports rather than undermines the claimed identification.

sections.title: Contingency, Determinism, and Necessity
sections.rationale: The first-stage argument depends on whether anything is genuinely contingent and whether causal determination differs from metaphysical necessity or instead transmits necessity through the causal chain.

sections.title: Explanatory Principle and Legitimate Stopping Points
sections.rationale: The competing burdens require determining why contingent existence calls for explanation and whether explanatory termination at God is principled when analogous termination at non-divine reality is proposed.

sections.title: Plurality, Composition, and External Explanation
sections.rationale: The central transition from explanations of individual contingent things to an explanation beyond their totality turns on composition, plurality, regress, convergence, and possible circularity concerns.

sections.title: Necessary Being or Necessary Universe
sections.rationale: Even if some necessary reality is granted, the motion requires comparison between a distinct necessary being and the option that the universe or lawful reality is itself necessary or brute.

sections.title: Identification with God and Explanatory Virtues
sections.rationale: The final motion-level inference requires grounds for divine attributes and tests whether perfection, simplicity, absence of arbitrary limits, and cumulative theistic considerations distinguish God from rival foundations.

chunk-001:c003.proposition: If reality has a necessary part and that necessary part is God, the first-stage conclusion combines with this identification to entail that God exists.

chunk-001:c005.proposition: A result can be causally determined without existing necessarily, because the determining system and its existence can still require explanation.

chunk-001:c006.proposition: Ordinary inquiry, scientific explanatory practice, inductive generalization, and the stable order of reality jointly support seeking explanations for contingent existence.

chunk-001:c007.proposition: Modal contingency, understood as the capacity to fail to exist, differs from existential dependence, though both notions can contribute to a contingency argument.

chunk-001:c009.proposition: Saying that a thing exists because it was determined to exist is circular if it leaves unexplained why the thing or determining arrangement exists.

chunk-002:chunk-002-candidate-04.proposition: Considering contingent things as a plurality avoids treating them as a further composed object, while separate explanations of every member still leave why that plurality exists unanswered.

chunk-002:chunk-002-candidate-08.proposition: The perfect-being and necessary-universe hypotheses can be compared abductively according to their respective explanatory virtues.

chunk-003:chunk003-candidate-01.proposition: A perfect necessary being is a maximally simple hypothesis, and that simplicity gives it greater intrinsic probability than more complex explanatory hypotheses.

chunk-003:chunk003-candidate-02.proposition: A perfect being avoids the unexplained arbitrary limits that would arise if a necessary foundation possessed only a particular finite degree of creative power.

chunk-003:chunk003-candidate-05.proposition: The plurality of all contingent things cannot explain itself, so its explanation must lie outside that plurality in a non-contingent and therefore necessary being.

chunk-001:c004.proposition: The argument must justify that apparently contingent things genuinely could have existed differently, because determinism may eliminate the modal alternatives required to classify them as contingent.

chunk-001:c010.proposition: If God's existence may be explained internally or treated as brute necessity, an equivalent explanatory stopping point must remain available for some non-divine reality unless a relevant difference is established.

chunk-002:chunk-002-candidate-01.proposition: If a necessary foundation necessarily produces the causal chain, necessity propagates through its effects, so every subsequent event in the universe occurs necessarily rather than contingently.

chunk-002:chunk-002-candidate-02.proposition: Rejecting self-causation as absurd does not support the argument unless the allegedly self-explanatory necessary existence of God is relevantly distinguished from the structure rejected elsewhere.

chunk-002:chunk-002-candidate-03.proposition: The explanatory needs of individual contingent members do not by themselves establish that their complete collection requires a further explanation, because that inference risks a fallacy of composition.

chunk-002:chunk-002-candidate-05.proposition: The camera-factory illustration does not establish a single external necessary source, because it either presupposes that separate explanatory chains converge on one source or permits them not to converge.

chunk-002:chunk-002-candidate-06.proposition: If determinism means there are no genuinely contingent things, the universe may itself be necessary and therefore need no additional necessary being beyond it as an explanation.

chunk-002:chunk-002-candidate-07.proposition: Labeling the necessary part of reality God does not establish a distinct perfect being, because the connection between necessary existence, perfection, and substantive divine attributes still requires argument.

chunk-002:chunk-002-candidate-09.proposition: Even if a necessary foundation is granted, the argument must show that God is more compelling than a necessary universe; parity between those alternatives does not justify the theistic conclusion.

chunk-003:chunk003-candidate-04.proposition: A brute universe governed by simple mathematical laws may be simpler than a willing God, whose will introduces further contingency and dependence questions rather than improving explanatory economy.
